entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen10271" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Adoration of the Omniscient and Omnipresent One</title> <div sID="gen10272" type="x-p"/> In this Aramaizing Psalm what the preceding Psalm says in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">Psa 139:6</reference> comes to be carried into effect, viz.: <hi type="italic">for Jahve is exalted and He seeth the lowly, and the proud He knoweth from afar</hi>. This Psalm has manifold points of contact with its predecessor. From a theological point of view it is one of the most instructive of the Psalms, and both as regards its contents and poetic character in every way worthy of David. But it is only inscribed לדוד because it is composed after the Davidic model, and is a counterpart to such Psalms as <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Psa 19:1-14</reference> and to other Davidic didactic Psalms. For the addition למנצח neither proves its ancient Davidic origin, nor in a general way its origin in the period prior to the Exile, as Ps 74 for example shows, which was at any rate not composed prior to the time of the Chaldaean catastrophe. <div eID="gen10272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10273" type="x-p"/> The Psalm falls into three parts: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Psa 139:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.13">Psa 139:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.19">Psa 139:19</reference>; the strophic arrangement is not clear. The first part celebrates the Omniscient and Omnipresent One. The poet knows that he is surrounded on all sides by God’s knowledge and His presence; His Spirit is everywhere and cannot be avoided; and His countenance is turned in every direction and inevitably, in wrath or in love. In the second part the poet continues this celebration with reference to the origin of man; and in the third part he turns in profound vexation of spirit towards the enemies of such a God, and supplicates for himself His proving and guidance. In <reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Psa 139:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.139.4">Psa 139:4</reference> God is called <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference> <hi type="italic">El</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.19">Psa 139:19</reference> <hi type="italic">Eloha</hi>, in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.21">Psa 139:21</reference> again <hi type="italic">Jahve</hi>, and in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.23">Psa 139:23</reference> again <hi type="italic">El</hi>. Strongly as this Psalm is marked by the depth and pristine freshness of its ideas and feeling, the form of its language is still such as is without precedent in the Davidic age. To all appearance it is the Aramaeo-Hebrew idiom of the post-exilic period pressed into the service of poetry. The Psalm apparently belongs to those Psalms which, in connection with a thoroughly classical character of form, bear marks of the influence which the Aramaic language of the Babylonian kingdom exerted over the exiles. This influence affected the popular dialect in the first instance, but the written language also did not escape it, as the Books of Daniel and Ezra show; and even the poetry of the Psalms is not without traces of this retrograde movement of the language of Israel towards the language of the patriarchal ancestral house. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.1-Ps.139.7">Psa 139:1-7</reference> <div eID="gen10273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10274" type="x-p"/> The Aramaic forms in this strophe are the ἅπαξ λεγομ רע (ground-form רעי) in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, endeavour, desire, thinking, like רעוּת and רעיון in the post-exilic books, from רעה (רעא), <hi type="italic">cupere, cogitare</hi>; and the ἅπ. λεγ. רבע in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.3">Psa 139:3</reference>, equivalent to רבץ, a lying down, if רבעי be not rather an infinitive like בּלעי in <reference osisRef="Job.7.19">Job 7:19</reference>, since ארחי is undoubtedly not inflected from ארח, but, as being infinitive, like עברי in <reference osisRef="Deut.4.21">Deu 4:21</reference>, from ארח; and the verb ארח also, with the exception of this passage, only occurs in the speeches of Elihu (<reference osisRef="Job.34.8">Job 34:8</reference>), which are almost more strongly Aramaizing than the Book of Job itself. Further, as an Aramaizing feature we have the objective relation marked by <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in the expression בּנתּה לרעי, Thou understandest my thinking, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">Psa 116:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.135.11">Psa 135:11</reference>; Psa 136:19. The monostichic opening is after the Davidic style, e.g., <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.23.1">Psa 23:1</reference></hi>. Among the prophets, Isaiah in particular is fond of such thematic introductions as we have here in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.1">Psa 139:1</reference></hi>. On ותּדע instead of ותּדעני vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.107.20">Psa 107:20</reference>; the pronominal object stands once beside the first verb, or even beside the second (2Ki 9:25), instead of twice (Hitzig). The “me” is then expanded: sitting down, rising up, walking and lying, are the sum of human conditions or states. רעי is the totality or sum of the life of the spirit and soul of man, and דּרכי the sum of human action. The divine knowledge, as ותּדע says, is the result of the scrutiny of man. The poet, however, in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.2">Psa 139:2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.139.3">Psa 139:3</reference> uses the perfect throughout as a mood of that which is practically existing, because that scrutiny is a scrutiny that is never unexecuted, and the knowledge is consequently an ever-present knowledge. מרחוק is meant to say that He sees into not merely the thought that is fully fashioned and matured, but even that which is being evolved. זרית from זרה is combined by Luther (with Azulai and others) with זר, <hi type="italic">a wreath</hi> (from זרר, <hi type="italic">constringere, cingere</hi>), inasmuch as he renders: whether I walk or lie down, Thou art round about me (<hi type="italic">Ich gehe oder lige , so bistu umb mich</hi>). זרה ought to have the same meaning here, if with Wetzstein one were to compare the Arabic, and more particularly Beduin, <hi type="italic">drrâ , dherrâ</hi>, to protect; the notion of affording protection does not accord with this train of thought, which has reference to God’s omniscience: what ought therefore to be meant is a hedging round which secures its object to the knowledge, or even a protecting that places it in security against any exchanging, which will not suffer the object to escape it.<note placement="foot">This <hi type="italic">Verb. tert.</hi> Arab. <hi type="italic">w et y</hi> is old, and the derivative <hi type="italic">dherâ</hi>, protection, is an elegant word; with reference to another derivative, <hi type="italic">dherwe</hi>, a wall of rock protecting one from the winds, vid., Job, at <reference osisRef="Job.24.7">Job 24:7</reference>, note. The II form (<hi type="italic">Piel</hi>) signifies to protect in the widest possible sense, e.g., (in <hi type="italic">Neshwân</hi>, ii. 343 <hi type="italic">b</hi>), “[Arab.] <hi type="italic">drâ 'l - šâh</hi>, he protected the sheep (against being exchanged) by leaving a lock of wool upon their backs when they were shorn, by which they might be recognised among other sheep.”</note> <div eID="gen10274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10275" type="x-p"/> The Arabic <hi type="italic">ḏrâ</hi>, to know, which is far removed in sound, is by no means to be compared; it is related to Arab. <hi type="italic">dr'</hi>, to push, urge forward, and denotes knowledge that is gained by testing and experimenting. But we also have no need of that Arab. <hi type="italic">ḏrâ</hi>, to protect, since we can remain within the range of the guaranteed Hebrew usage, inasmuch as זרה, to winnow, i.e., to spread out that which has been threshed and expose it to the current of the wind, in Arabic likewise <hi type="italic">ḏrrâ</hi>, (whence מזרה, <hi type="italic">midhrâ</hi>, a winnowing-fork, like רחת, <hi type="italic">racht</hi>, a winnowing-shovel), gives an appropriate metaphor. Here it is equivalent to: to investigate and search out to the very bottom; lxx, Symmachus, and Theodotion, ἐξιξηνίασας, after which the Italic renders <hi type="italic">investigasti</hi>, and Jerome <hi type="italic">eventilasti</hi>. הסכּין with the accusative, as in <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference> with עם: to enter into neighbourly, close, familiar relationship, or to stand in such relationship, with any one; cogn. שׁכן, Arab. <hi type="italic">skn</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Ps.139.5">Psa 139:5</reference> Luther has been misled by the lxx and Vulgate, which take צוּר in the signification <hi type="italic">formare</hi> (whence צוּרה, <hi type="italic">forma</hi>); it signifies, as the definition “behind and before” shows, to surround, encompass. God is acquainted with man, for He holds him surrounded on all sides, and man can do nothing, if God, whose confining hand he has lying upon him (<reference osisRef="Job.9.23">Job 9:23</reference>), does not allow him the requisite freedom of motion. Instead of דּעתּך (XX ἡ γνῶσίς σου) the poet purposely says in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.6">Psa 139:6</reference></hi> merely דּעת: a knowledge, so all-penetrating, all-comprehensive as God’s knowledge. The <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> reads פּליאה, but the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> פּלאיּה is supported by the <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> פּלאי in Jdg 13:18, the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> of which there is not פּליא, but פּלי (the pausal form of an adjective פּלי, the feminine of which would be פּליּה). With ממּנּי the transcendence, with נשׂגּבה the unattainableness, and with להּ לא־אוּכל the incomprehensibleness of the fact of the omniscience of God is expressed, and with this, to the mind of the poet, coincides God’s omnipresence; for true, not merely phenomenal, knowledge is not possible without the immanence of the knowing one in the thing known. God, however, is omnipresent, sustaining the life of all things by His Spirit, and revealing Himself either in love or in wrath - what the poet styles His countenance. To flee from this omnipresence (מן, away from), as the sinner and he who is conscious of his guilt would gladly do, is impossible. Concerning the first אנּה, which is here accented on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi>, vid., on Psa 116:4.

God, however, is omnipresent, sustaining the life of all things by His Spirit, and revealing Himself either in love or in wrath - what the poet styles His countenance. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.13-Ps.139.18">Psa 139:13-18</reference> <div eID="gen10277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10278" type="x-p"/> The fact that man is manifest to God even to the very bottom of his nature, and in every place, is now confirmed from the origin of man. The development of the child in the womb was looked upon by the Israelitish Chokma as one of the greatest mysteries, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Ecc 11:5</reference>; and here the poet praises this coming into being as a marvellous work of the omniscient and omnipresent omnipotence of God. קנה here signifies <hi type="italic">condere</hi>; and סכך not: to cover, protect, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.140.8">Psa 140:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.40.22">Job 40:22</reference>, prop. to cover with network, to hedge in, but: to plait, interweave, viz., with bones, sinews, and veins, like שׂכך in Job 10:11. The reins are made specially prominent in order to mark the, the seat of the tenderest, most secret emotions, as the work of Him who trieth the heart and the reins. The προσευχή becomes in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.14">Psa 139:14</reference> the εὐχαριστία: I give thanks unto Thee that I have wonderfully come into being under fearful circumstances, i.e., circumstances exciting a shudder, viz., of astonishment (נוראות as in <reference osisRef="Ps.65.6">Psa 65:6</reference>). נפלה (= נפלא) is the passive to הפלה, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>; Psa 17:7. Hitzig regards נפליתה (Thou hast shown Thyself wonderful), after the lxx, Syriac, Vulgate, and Jerome, as the only correct reading; but the thought which is thereby gained comes indeed to be expressed in the following line, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.139.14">Psa 139:14</reference></hi>, which sinks down into tautology in connection with this reading. `otsem (collectively equivalent to עצמים, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.5">Ecc 11:5</reference>) is the bones, the skeleton, and, starting from that idea, more generally the state of being as a sum-total of elements of being. אשׁר, without being necessarily a conjunction (Ew. §333, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), attaches itself to the suffix of עצמי. רקּם, “to be worked in different colours, or also embroidered,” of the system of veins ramifying the body, and of the variegated colouring of its individual members, more particularly of the inward parts; perhaps, however, more generally with a retrospective conception of the colours of the outline following the undeveloped beginning, and of the forming of the members and of the organism in general.<note placement="foot">In the Talmud the egg of a bird or of a reptile is called מרקּמת, when the outlines of the developed embryo are visible in it; and likewise the mole (<hi type="italic">mola</hi>), when traces of human; organization can be discerned in it.</note> <div eID="gen10278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10279" type="x-p"/> The mother’s womb is here called not merely סתר (cf. Aeschylus’ <hi type="italic">Eumenides</hi>, 665: ἐν σκοτοισι νηδύος τεθραμμένη, and the designation of the place where the foetus is formed as “a threefold darkness’ in the Koran, <hi type="italic">Sur</hi>. xxxix. 8), the <hi type="italic">ē</hi> of which is retained here in pause (vid., Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Lehrbuch</hi>, §298), but by a bolder appellation תּחתּיּות ארץ, the lowest parts of the earth, i.e., the interior of the earth (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.63.10">Psa 63:10</reference>) as being the secret laboratory of the earthly origin, with the same retrospective reference to the first formation of the human body out of the dust of the earth, as when Job says,  <reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference> : “naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return thither” -  שׁמּה, viz., εἰς τὴν γῆν τὴν μητέρα πάντων, Sir. 40:1. The interior of Hades is also called בּטן שׁאול in <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jon 2:2</reference>, Sir. 51:5. According to the view of Scripture the mode of Adam’s creation is repeated in the formation of every man, <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job 33:6</reference>, cf. Job 33:4. The earth was the mother’s womb of Adam, and the mother’s womb out of which the child of Adam comes forth is the earth out of which it is taken.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Ps.139.23-Ps.139.24">Psa 139:23-24</reference> <div eID="gen10284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10285" type="x-p"/> He sees in them the danger which threatens himself, and prays God not to give him over to the judgment of self-delusion, but to lay bare the true state of his soul. The fact “Thou hast searched me,” which the beginning of the Psalm confesses, is here turned into a petitioning “search me.” Instead of רעים in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.17">Psa 139:17</reference>, the poet here says שׂרעפּים, which signifies branches (<reference osisRef="Ezek.31.5">Eze 31:5</reference>) and branchings of the act of thinking (thoughts and cares, <reference osisRef="Ps.94.19">Psa 94:19</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Resh</hi> is epenthetic, for the first form is שׂעפּים, <reference osisRef="Job.4.13">Job 4:13</reference>; Job 20:2. The poet thus sets the very ground and life of his heart, with all its outward manifestations, in the light of the divine omniscience. And in <reference osisRef="Ps.139.24">Psa 139:24</reference> he prays that God would see whether any דּרך־עצב cleaves to him (בּי as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.24">1Sa 25:24</reference>), by which is not meant “a way of idols” (Rosenmüller, Gesenius, and Maurer), after <reference osisRef="Isa.48.5">Isa 48:5</reference>, since an inclination towards, or even apostasy to, heathenism cannot be an unknown sin; nor to a man like the writer of this Psalm is heathenism any power of temptation. דוך בּצע (Grätz) might more readily be admissible, but דוך עצב is a more comprehensive notion, and one more in accordance with this closing petition. The poet gives this name to the way that leads to the pain, torture, viz., of the inward and outward punishments of sin; and, on the other hand, the way along which he wishes to be guided he calls דּרך עולם, the way of endless continuance (lxx, Vulgate, Luther), not the way of the former times, after <reference osisRef="Jer.6.16">Jer 6:16</reference> (Maurer, Olshausen), which thus by itself is ambiguous (as becomes evident from <reference osisRef="Job.22.15">Job 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.18.15">Jer 18:15</reference>), and also does not furnish any direct antithesis. The “everlasting way” is the way of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.27.11">Psa 27:11</reference>), the way of the righteous, which stands fast for ever and shall not “perish” (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.6">Psa 1:6</reference>).  <chapter eID="Ps.139"/> <div eID="gen10285" type="x-p"/>
